memoryText: The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Ecclesiastes 12:13 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the Preacher’s final answer. After twelve chapters of searching, he arrives at a conclusion that is as simple as it is demanding.

“The end of the matter; all has been heard.” The Preacher says that he has finished. All the observations, experiments, and puzzles have been laid out. Now comes the summary. It is a way of saying: if you want only one thing from this book, take this.

“Fear God.” The book began with “vanity,” and it ends with “fear.” The Preacher’s long reflection shows that nothing under the sun can bear the weight of our hopes. The only stable footing is a right relationship to the God who made us. To fear God is to honor him as God, to trust him, to submit to him, and to take him seriously.

“And keep his commandments.” Fear is not just a feeling. It shows itself in obedience. The two belong together. A person who says he fears God but ignores what God says has not understood.

“For this is the whole duty of man.” The Hebrew is literally “this is the whole of man.” This is what a human being is for. It is the purpose of our existence. All the things we chase, if they are not oriented to this, are a breath.

The verse that follows adds a motive: God will bring every deed into judgment. This is both a warning and a comfort. Nothing is hidden, and nothing is wasted. For the Christian, the weight of this verse is carried by Christ. He kept God’s commandments perfectly, and he bore the judgment we deserved. We now fear God not as condemned people but as forgiven children, and we obey out of gratitude. Pray this verse as a summary of your life’s purpose.
weekInReview: This week you moved from Proverbs into the heart of Ecclesiastes. You saw the Preacher’s verdict on life under the sun: vanity of vanities, a breath. You read the poem of times and the promise that God has put eternity into our hearts. You read the Psalter’s answers to the same questions: Psalm 49, in which God ransoms the soul from Sheol, and Psalm 73, where the psalmist’s near-slip ended in the sanctuary and in the great confession, “Whom have I in heaven but you?” You followed the Preacher’s counsel on worship, wealth, mourning, and mortality, and his call to enjoy life as a gift and to work with all your might. And you reached the end of the matter: fear God and keep his commandments. The week taught that nothing under the sun satisfies, that death is real, and that God himself is our portion.
reflectionQuestions: The Preacher says God has “put eternity into man’s heart.” Where do you feel that longing for something more, and how does it point you to God?
Psalm 49 says no one can ransom another, but God will ransom the faithful from Sheol. How does Jesus fulfill this promise, and how does it change how you think about death?
Psalm 73 says, “Whom have I in heaven but you?” If you honestly answer that question today, what do you find?
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to fear him and keep his commandments.
Rest in him as the strength of your heart.
